extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning mathematical proof techniques / introductory proof course
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples for proving existential and uniqueness statements and other standard proof types (biconditionals, cases, epsilon–delta limits, set equalities, Cartesian products). Emphasizes proof strategies, template structure, and typical manipulations of quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove 4!x P(x) via existence and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form 4!x P(x): Prove dx P(x) and VyVz((P(y) A P(z)) > y = z). The two parts of the proof are therefore sometimes labeled existence and uniqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of final proof: Existence: [Proof of 4x P(x) goes here.] Uniqueness: [Proof of VyVz((P(y) A P(z)) > y = z) goes here.]. For existence, find (exhibit) a witness x making P(x) true. For uniqueness, let y and z be arbitrary, assume P(y) and P(z), and prove y = z. Example: choose A = ∅ to show existence in set-union uniqueness problems; show usage in Example 3.6.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative equivalent formulations of 4!x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several other formulas are equivalent to 4!x P(x), e.g. Ax(P(x) A Vy(P(y) > y = x)), AxVy(P(y) = y = x), dx P(x) A VyVz((P(y) A P(z)) > y = z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving any one of these equivalents suffices to show 4!x P(x). Use different equivalents as they suggest different proof approaches; statement 3 (existence & uniqueness conjunct) is most commonly used in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existential instantiation (choose a name for a witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have an existential given, choose a name (e.g. x0) for some object satisfying the existential and reason with that name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from dx P(x) let x0 be such that P(x0). Treat x0 as a given throughout the subproof. Scratch work that found x0 need not appear in the final proof; final proof simply states the witness and verifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a given of the form 4!x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 4!x P(x) as two separate givens: 4x P(x) and VyVz((P(y) A P(z)) > y = z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use the existence half, choose a witness name x0 such that P(x0). To use the uniqueness half, whenever two objects both satisfy P, you may conclude they are equal. Example: in Example 3.6.4, pick b and c from nonempty intersections and use uniqueness to conclude b = c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving several statements equivalent via a cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of proving every pairwise biconditional, prove a chain of implications (e.g. 1 => 2, 2 => 3, 3 => 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the number of conditionals you must prove (three conditionals instead of six in a three-statement equivalence). Use conditional proofs for each link; remaining biconditionals follow by transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting negated quantified statements into positive form
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantifier-negation and propositional equivalences to convert negated existential/universal claims into positive statements (e.g. aAy(P(y) Ay # x) equivalent steps shown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantifier negation law, DeMorgan’s law, and conditional law to transform ~dx P(x) into Vy(P(y) -> y = x) or other convenient forms. This can turn a proof of a negated statement into a proof of an equivalent positive statement that is easier to handle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential proof template (exhibit a witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an existential statement 4x P(x), find a specific value and prove P(that_value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratch work to find the witness is fine but should not appear in final proof. The final proof states the chosen witness and demonstrates P(witness). Example: in Example 3.6.2 choose A = ∅ and verify VB(∅ ∪ B = B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness VyVz((P(y) A P(z)) > y = z): let y and z be arbitrary, assume P(y) and P(z), and prove y = z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often paired with an existence proof; label the two parts 'Existence' and 'Uniqueness'. Example: use plugging-in of appropriate values and givens to deduce equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using universal givens: choose clever substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a universal statement Vx P(x), you will usually plug in a particular value for x; sometimes a clever choice is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what goal you need and choose the substitution to make the given useful (examples: plug in x0 to get P(x0); in set proofs plug in other sets as choices for B to obtain CU D = D etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases for disjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a disjunction (A or B), handle each case separately proving the goal in both branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Euclid-style prime proof, m is either prime or a product of primes — treat each as a case and show both produce a contradiction or the required object. Label cases explicitly or reason by cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for negative/existence-of-counterexample statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a negative statement (e.g. 'there are infinitely many primes' = not finite), assume the negation and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate finiteness/infiniteness into existential/universal logical form before applying contradiction. Example: assume a finite list of primes, construct m = product + 1 and consider divisibility to contradict completeness of list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–delta limit proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a limit statement lim_{x->c} f(x) = L, follow the quantifier structure: let ε>0 be arbitrary, find δ>0 (often depending on ε), let x be arbitrary with 0<|x−c|<δ, then show |f(x) − L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out algebraic manipulation to express |f(x) − L| in terms of |x−c| during scratch work; choose δ accordingly (e.g. δ = ε/2 in example). Present only the chosen δ and verification in the final proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equalities: two standard approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A = B you can (a) show ∀p [p ∈ A ↔ p ∈ B] elementwise, or (b) show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A (i.e., prove two inclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common proof pattern: start with an arbitrary element of one side and prove membership of the other; when inclusions are used, do both directions. Commentary notes both approaches are natural and show examples (Theorem 4.1.3 proof used two inclusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with Cartesian products: treat elements as ordered pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements about A × B, start with an arbitrary element which is an ordered pair (x,y) with x ∈ A and y ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often authors suppress explicit unpacking of ordered-pair membership and simply write (x,y) from the outset. Use this to reason coordinatewise (e.g. prove x ∈ A and y ∈ B to show (x,y) ∈ A×B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scratch work vs final proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Scratch work (algebraic solving, discovery of witnesses, manipulative steps) is useful for finding how to construct a proof but should generally not appear in the polished final proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated repeatedly: showing how a witness was discovered is fine while doing scratch work, but the final proof simply states the witness and verifies the required properties. Examples: solving 2y/(y+1)=x for y to find witness; choosing x and y formulas in Theorem 3.7.1.
